John LaBarbera

John LaBarbera’s compositions and arrangements have been performed by Buddy Rich, Woody Herman, Count Basie, and the Glenn Miller Orchestra. His scoring credits include TV and radio spots for Kodak and Xerox; and his published charts are considered standards in the field of jazz education.
John was interviewed via Zoom on July 13, 2021 by Monk Rowe, Director of the Fillius Jazz Archive.

My name is Monk Rowe for the Fillius Jazz Archive at Hamilton College. I’m very pleased to have John LaBarbera with me today. I’m going to introduce you as first a fourth trumpeter, composer/arranger, and I’m very glad to have you here because I love talking about composing and arranging.
Well thanks, Monk. I’ve watched your interviews with a number of folks, including my brother Pat, and you know, I really enjoy being a part of this. Really.

Excellent. I’m not going to spend a lot of time on this but I had a couple of thoughts and questions about the family band. For those of you who might be watching we have three brothers and your father and mother were also in the group. Is that correct?
Yes that’s right.
And how old were you during the years that this band was active?

I think I started when I was six or seven. If Pat was eight then I was six. And Joe would have been, oh no, I think I was seven and Joe was five, or four. I’m sorry. Joe was four or five. Somewhere along in that line. It’s hard to remember because we were always playing. The family band came much — but my mother at first was not part of the band as you probably know from Pat. But I think when I was about eight we were gigging steadily as a family band.
Did your father write parts for your trumpet playing that — with the fact that you’re seven or eight?

No, no. We just played stock arrangements. We didn’t ease into it. I mean they weren’t that difficult, the stocks weren’t that difficult but we started right out playing stocks. He wrote some polka things out that — he would transcribe some polka parts for the trumpet that were originally for me, and he made the clarinet or mandolin — Pat would play clarinet and I would play, well during those — when we played the polkas I played piano most of the time. But he would copy some parts, yeah, for trumpet, but not a lot.
For the folks who don’t know, can you explain what stocks means?
Oh, well, these were dance band arrangements. They were called convertible arrangements. I called them contemptible, contemptible, but anyway these arrangements © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

were written for a typical society dance band which included violin; piano, bass and drums; saxophones, so you would have your first alto, your second tenor, and the third part would be baritone sometimes. All right? And two trumpets and one trombone. Usually. And they were expandable, also expendable. So you could play them with a trumpet and an alto saxophone, first trumpet and first alto, and rhythm section, and they would sound. But then you could add all those other instruments and they’d sound fuller. And this is the type of arranging that we used to use for the Catskill Mountain singers you know, they want to play it with a trio and a full big band. It’s got to be expandable. And it’s a certain technique that was — Spud Murphy, Johnny Warrington, all those guys could write these things, Van Alexander. And they were quite popular. And my father, we would go every week to Rochester, New York to Levitt’s Music and he would buy more stocks, whatever the popular tune was, and we’d play it. I’ve got them all in my garage.
No kidding.
Oh yeah. Hundreds.
So in the future you can have another band playing the stocks. I remember seeing those names you mentioned in junior high, we called it the stage band.
Yeah. You had to call it the stage band, yeah.

Now there is a certain skill I guess, a formulatic skill to writing in that fashion. I’m wondering, I looked up just before we joined today some of the top popular songs in 1957. So would you get requests, people coming up to the band and saying, “Hey, can you play ‘Raunchy’ or can you play ‘Sleepwalk’ or how about some Elvis Presley?”

We would get that occasionally but it was rare. It was rare for the clientele that we were playing for. I think we had a couple of rock & roll things that were, you know, popular, also the “Hucklebuck,” you know popular dance kind of things. But nothing really current for that period. I mean you have to remember that also in that period people were singing “Oh My Papa” and things like that were in parallel universe with the Elvis Presleys and the others.

That’s a terrific way to say that and I’ve been fascinated by that, because when you look at the top ten from a particular month and week in the mid-50s you see exactly that. Mitch Miller followed by Elvis or the other way around. It’s really fascinating.
Yeah. And you remember the Hit Parade of course, that would give you the top ten or top fifteen. Well Pop also bought these books. They were combo books called “Combo Orks.”
Combo Orks.
And they would have like the hit tunes and it was a cheap and dirty way of you know playing with a small band and covering those. So we would have a whole pile of music © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-
with us and if someone had a request and we had it, bam, we’d come out and we’d play it. It was good training.
Let’s suppose you had a week in the summer and you played three gigs. What kind of money would you expect from your father, individually?

Originally I think we got three dollars, then it went up to five dollars. You know we were buying our own comic books when we were in school and we had more money than anybody in my class. Because you remember, five bucks back in the 50s was a considerable allowance. Most kids were getting 25 cents or 50 cents as an allowance if they got an allowance.

Do you remember if at some point, you mentioned the stock arrangements, and you’re playing all this different music. Did you have this epiphany or an aha moment, like I could do this? I could arrange. I want to do that.

Well I don’t know if it really was an epiphany moment but I remember when we started getting interested in jazz, real jazz, not the Dixieland or the swing stuff that we were playing as kids, when we got into high school and we all of a sudden heard Miles Davis and we heard all of these great artists, I was the one who took them off the records. I have, for some reason I have the ability to hear all those inner lines and then write them down. I was the one who did that. So we could copy “So What” you know the Miles Davis group with the three horns or two horns, and I would copy all the notes off and write them out. So I was in the habit of doing that. But really we didn’t listen to big bands at all. I mean not at all, but we listened to some Glenn Miller and stuff like that, Stan Kenton. But I really didn’t get into big bands until I got into college, when I heard, you know, toward the end of my senior year I started hearing “Woody Herman ‘63” and we saw Woody Herman’s band live, and “Maynard ’61,” all those bands and it really had a big effect on me for some reason, it just grabbed me, and maybe because I had the ability to hear some of that inner stuff then I gravitated toward that kind of writing, although originally it was all small bands for us.
Was your father, I’m not sure how to put this, was he living out a way of life that he wished he had had as a professional musician?

Could be. It’s very possible. Because you know he never had a childhood and he made sure that we had a real childhood and really had a family unit, which, you know, he was in an orphanage for a while so he made sure that we were in a good family unit and he told me that when he had three sons, you know that was a big deal having three sons, originally, because he did all kinds of carpentry and odd jobs. He figured he could have his own construction company with three boys, three sons, you could really do well. But he also gave us the music. So you know he didn’t have money so basically he gave us that opportunity. And you’ve got to remember, being a musician back then was not a real © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

job. No one thought you could make a living doing that. But he made sure that we had that foundation. Of course then when we went off on our own and started playing without the family band, you know, we were making money and gigging so I think he was kind of pleased about that. And I’m sure he would have loved to have been a professional out in the real world, out in the world, but he had so many bands in the area. He had marching bands, he had concert bands, dance bands, you name it. So he had bands for every occasion. When Mussolini’s brown shirts came to Mount Morris, he called ahead and found “Giovinezza” which was the theme song from Mussolini’s youth, the youth, Giovinezza, the youth. And when the brown shirts were marching down the street of Mount Morris he had the band start playing that and they were shocked and they gave the old salute to Mussolini. They were staying in Dansville at the McFadden mansion. He was a real right winger. I don’t know if you remember that.
I do — that’s the first I’ve heard about brown shirts anywhere in New York State.

Yeah, was it the brown shirts or the black shirts? I think it was the brown shirts. Whatever Mussolini’s youth group was. And this McFadden had a huge resort in Dansville, kind of a weird medical kind of a colon-cleansing and all that, he invited them to the United States before we got involved and all that. But Pop was always on top of things. He had that theme song. I’ve probably got it out in the garage. But no one even knew what that was.
What finally, everybody got older and was there a particular thing that caused the family band to go the way of all bands, eventually it has to end somewhere.

Well we were getting more into jazz and we were in high school, and we didn’t have the kind of time when we were in grade school to go out and gig all the time. Plus I think my parents were happy to have some time alone at home and get rid of the kids, get us out the door.
What role did your Italian heritage have in this whole thing? I noticed that you were written about in a new book about jazz musicians and the Italian heritage.

Well you know we were, we were in a town that was mostly Irish American and we were the Sicilians. And we were pretty low on the totem pole. But it wasn’t in your face every day, because our group was pretty much among our ethnic neighbors and family. But you know the Italian thing I never really thought about it until I got into college. I didn’t know I was Italian until I got to college and someone called me a name. You know really, because we never thought about that. Everybody had a name like ours in our town except for the others, the other side. And I’m not being jive about this but I really didn’t think about that race thing because we weren’t raised as, you’ve got to remember my father came from Sicily so the racism was not bare, fundamentally there was nothing there. But when I got to college, well you meet all kinds of people in college and, you know, we © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

were talking about Hal, that’s where I first met Hal. I think he was the very first black friend I’ve ever had in my life. Because in Mount Morris I think there was one black family. I think. Yeah, there was one black family in Mount Morris. Yeah.
What would have happened, I think Pat said that he gave me a little anecdote and he discovered improvising because he couldn’t see the music to play the written out solo.

Yeah the Ted Mack Amateur Hour audition — or there was a contest at one of the — I can’t remember what it was but it was at a county fair and they had a contest and we entered it. And Pat, I guess the music either blew away or he couldn’t see it. And he had that — that was an epiphany because he made it up. And then we realized that that was a thing. But you know there was no books, there were no books at that period like you can get today. So we would try to copy — we didn’t try we did, we copied solos off the record and then we’d take Pop’s fake books and see what the chord changes were, which were very poor changes, and try to figure out why did Lee Morgan play that E flat on a C 7 chord. It’s like what is this?
You were doing like second year jazz education. I mean that is such great ear training to discover that on your own.

Yeah it is. Because again, I mean they had these books like hot jazz solos that were written out, you know, make believe solos by somebody and Charlie Colin, Charles Colin used to publish those, and those were a rarity. I mean we’d get our hands on those it’d be nice. But they really didn’t give you, they were pretty diatonic. They didn’t give you the real deal. You know you hear Miles Davis play on some of these tunes, even on a blues, you know what was that all about? You know your ears think wow, it works but why?
Yes. And if I play the same thing is it going to work as well as that.
And we all copied solos. Pat’s still got all the solos in books that he copied. But that’s the way you learn. You have to learn by copying and then hopefully your own thing comes out.
Do you feel like you developed your own thing on the trumpet?

No not really. I think I had up to about some great Lee Morgan licks up until the 60s. But you know trumpet was a way of staying in music and making some money, but I really didn’t have that fire like Pat has or Joe has for the instrument. Because when writing took over, I really didn’t, you know I’ve got a trumpet back there somewhere but you know it’s not my passion. I like playing it, it’s fun. But I really didn’t have that fire to continue on like Pat did and really get into it. Because again, the writing took over.
So you became a writer, you’re dependent on whether people play your music.
Yup.
How do you — what was your entrance like into that world? © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

Well Buddy Rich of course put me on the map. You know I played trumpet on Buddy’s band for about four months. He fired me a couple of times, at least a couple of times. But I learned a lot on that band. Of course playing in bands, like with my parents with our family band, you understand how things work. You hear the melody then you hear the counter line. And when I was playing in college, when I played in big bands in college, I had my own big band in Potsdam. Well you get to hear all those inner voicings and inner workings. And that’s why single line instrumentalists make the best arrangers. Piano players and guitar players are the hardest people to teach. But a single line instrument — let me put it this way — a non-breathing player, a non-breathing instrument player has the hardest time writing, because they don’t have to breathe. But a horn player or a wind player, put it that way, are the people who really get it quickly. You know like Billy Byers and Slide Hampton, we can go right down — Bill Holman, go right down on the list. But I forgot where we were going with this.
Well I wondered how you, like if there was a real door that opened you, for your composing and I think you said Buddy Rich because you came back and started writing for him, is that correct?

Yes. I enjoyed the band. You know he respected me and if he respected you he would take a chance on you — if he respected you as a player he’d take a chance on you as a writer. That’s why a lot of the guys in the band were writing charts for the band, because he respected their playing and he would listen to what they had to write. Well I was on the Glenn Miller band for three years, almost three years with Buddy DeFranco. And I learned a lot from him as well. So all the time I was on the Glenn Miller band I was writing arrangements, I was transcribing the Miller stuff off the 78 recordings, because a lot of that music disappeared. The real arrangements disappeared. And a lot — I mean we had the library in New York City which I’d go through, all the Bill Finegan stuff, but a lot of times I was transcribing from a 78 recording on a cassette tape in the back of the bus. Anyway, so I made all my mistakes on the Glenn Miller band. And then we were in England on tour and I said I can’t do this. Because I looked across the aisle at an alto player named, oh God, why can’t I think of his name, it’ll come back to me. He’d been on the band with every road band there was, Al Thompson. He was a second alto player. He played in every band and that’s all he did. He was an alcoholic and I looked across and I said that could be me, you know, at the end of my life just sitting there on the damn band bus, you know, playing one-nighters. So I gave my notice in England and I was back in Rochester on unemployment. A lot of people helped us out like for instance Vince Falcone who was Frank Sinatra’s accompanist. He ran a piano company, the Shale Piano Company in Rochester. And he would give us the pianos the people traded in. He gave Chuck Mangione one, he gave Pat one, he gave me one. He’d have the guys deliver © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

it to your apartment, because you know it’s not worth anything, it’s just like a used car, they’ll give you so much for the trade in. Anyway, long story short, I was on unemployment and I heard that Buddy had signed, Pat told me that Buddy had signed with RCA Victor. And so I was making fifty bucks a week on unemployment and then doing odd jobs. A bus trip to Philadelphia was 25 bucks. So I bought a bus ticket to Philadelphia with this “Piece of the Road” suite that I wrote. And everybody was there at the club, Brandy’s Wharf in Philadelphia. You know Don Sebesky, all the guys were there with charts. So it was a cattle call. So I was there, put on the chart down, I’ve actually got a cassette of the rehearsal, and you know Buddy didn’t play he just sat there. And there was a, they started with a ballad which was unusual for Jimmy Mosher, and then there was a rock piece, and then a solo piano and then a jazz waltz. When we got to the jazz waltz part, after about, I don’t know maybe about half the chart, maybe not even half the chart, he stopped. And he went and sat down at the drums and played it. And at the end he says, “Okay, I want you in New York in a couple of weeks and we’re going to record your stuff.” Just like that. And you know I said, “Yeah, sure, right.” You know. But that was it. He said, “You’re in.” And you know I’ve told this story before but that really put me on the map, writing for Buddy Rich. I mean you can’t get any bigger than that.
Man, I bet your made sure that the parts were all correct. I mean did you do the copying by yourself at that time?

You would think I would do that. You would think I would make all kinds of painful reviewing. But luckily a lot of the guys in the band were my friends and they corrected a lot of mistakes for me. The parts were in pencil. The parts were in pencil. However, when we finally got to the RCA Victor recording, this was in the old days when the record companies paid for the copyist, they paid the composer and the arranger, everything was union scale. So I was on the road with a man named Milt Newman who had worked as a copyist. He taught me how to copy. But then I befriended a good colleague of his, Larry Abel, who became my copyist for years. And he did all the copying and it was all done you know, the right way, and the record company paid for it. The copyist got residuals.
Oh no kidding?
Yeah.
Wow. What did you expect from him? Did you trust him to come to you and say, “Listen John, measure 46 you’ve got this note that, I don’t think it’s what you want. Would he do that?

No he would just say something’s wrong there. Or I don’t like that section cut it out. And you’d have to do it. It’s like Mancini said, it’s like giving up one of your children but you © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-
have to do it, you can’t fall in love with every note you write. Because he knows more than you do about what he’s presenting.
Wow.
Yeah.
He hadn’t heard it yet.
No.
But he could tell by looking at it.

He could tell by hearing it. You know we rehearsed the whole thing. He couldn’t read music but he must have had this second sense of the whole picture. For instance you know my CD “On the Wild Side” I recorded “Walk on the Wild Side” the whole suite. I wrote that for Buddy. And he played it but he never got to record it before he died. And when I brought it into him there’s a Dixieland section in there that Elmer Bernstein had in the film. He cut the entire thing out. And I was pissed. But it works that way and so when I recorded it myself I did it the way he wanted it. Because he could tell what the — you know he could tell, all right, by this point the audience is getting itchy. They’re going to want the drum solo, they’re going to want something big. You can’t drag it on after a ballad and have a Dixieland thing. Or whatever. You know, that kind of sense.
Did you ever write a Buddy Rich chart that didn’t have a drum solo that he said, “Okay we’ve got to put in a drum solo.”

Never. And I did a lot of things that weren’t drum solos and he liked them. See one thing about writing for Buddy Rich, I wrote for — I’ve written for the other bands, Buddy did not have a style. People could argue that he did, but he didn’t have a style. You could bring any kind of chart into Buddy and he would try it. He may not like it, he may not use it, but he had a voracious appetite for new material. That’s — my brother Pat hipped me to the fact that never bring anything in two weeks or two months or three months before the recording session. Bring it in at the last minute because he’s tired of that other stuff, he wants new stuff. And for subsequent records I did that, I brought in, you know we were going to record in London and two weeks before we went to London I brought in all that stuff and he said, “All right, let’s go to London and record it.”
So that would get played live maybe a few times before the session. But not too many times.

Yes. Not too many times, because again, he’d get bored. And although he did have his favorites and he had things he had to play like “West Side Story” or “Channel One Suite,” things the audience expected. Like Woody Herman had to play “Woodchopper’s Ball.” You had your little hits and you had to make sure you fulfilled that requirement for the audience. © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

I wonder if you had a feeling and other composer/arrangers have this feeling that I’m writing this chart for Buddy Rich but I want it to be something that other bands will want to play or that I can market to the educational field, and how do I walk that line?

I couldn’t think that way because the stuff that I’d write for Buddy Rich would be too hard for college bands and high school bands to play. And there really wasn’t a market for real professional charts. So when you talk about Hal Leonard or Kendor or any of the publishing companies, they had a level of proficiency that they stuck with for colleges and for high schools. A grade level. Now some of the things that I ended up publishing were kind of scaled down for that market, when I finally did decide to start selling them in the, you know, educational field. But I always, when I was writing for the band I was writing for that band, I wasn’t going to short-change it and try and water it down so it had a second level of, you know, commerciality.
Did you have a way of determining a price for your work and how did it change over the years?

That’s a rough one. That is hard. Because you never know what to charge. You know the worst thing you can hear a producer say is, “Thank you for being so reasonable.” That’s the last thing you want to hear. You know what? You get a sense of what the bandleader or the client can pay. You get a sense, and you hit them with a figure. And you just hope they will come back with something, or they don’t say get lost. It’s hard. Because you know every market is different. Like for Buddy Rich a lot of people don’t know this but I rarely got paid by Buddy. A lot of stuff I had to scream and yell trying to get paid. He didn’t have the money. He was used to, as a star, having anything he wanted. He just would spend — I’ll buy this — and a lot of times the manager didn’t have the money to pay me. And when I had friends that were managers, like Stanley Kay, he would go to bat for me, he’d find the money somewhere. He’d maybe take an extra couple of hundred here. But having said that, Buddy gave me all of the publishing rights to everything I had done for him. He knew, he knew that was a valuable thing. Woody Herman didn’t. Maynard Ferguson didn’t. Count Basie didn’t. They would grab the publishing, as rightfully they should. Buddy gave me a hundred percent of everything. So that was the payback. It was rough at the time but you know, the payback is there.
Did you ever have a manager or bandleader say, “Come on, John, this would be good exposure for you”?

Yeah. I had that happen. I had a record company out in California, one of Woody’s recordings. The guy said, “Well we don’t pay that kind of money for arrangements” and you know, “this is something you should be happy, you’re going to get your stuff on a Woody Herman record.” Yeah. I’ve got stories. There’s a lot of stories out there. © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-
You mentioned your stint with Glenn Miller and you made your arranging mistakes then. What were the arranging mistakes that you learned about and didn’t do later?

Writing too much. Just writing everything. You know I’ll back up and say that the first symphony I heard was at Geneseo State Teacher’s College. My father and mother took us to see an orchestra, the Rochester Symphony. And I’d never heard anything like that in my life. And I hadn’t heard a real full big band at that point either, right? You know that was the first large ensemble live that I heard. You know in high school we had concert bands and all that. But anyway, when they took a break I looked at the stage and I could hear all of those instruments, just looking at the music stands. Now it sounds kind of stupid but when I first went on Buddy’s band and I would sit there and in the band itself that didn’t happen. But when I stood in front of a band, or sat in front of a band, and the band took a break, if I looked at the music stands I could hear all the music. Now I don’t need to look at the music stands, I found, with the Glenn Miller band, that you know I can hear the whole package. But the problem is is that you don’t have the experience of editing. I think maybe Bill Holman said it, you know, you write all your life and toward the end of your career you learn how to take stuff away, how to not put it down in the first place, how to not write. So I was writing too busily and too much stuff. And of course Buddy DeFranco would give me criticisms and comments like that because he worked with everybody. And a lot of it took hold. And then by studying the Glenn Miller scores, like Bill Finegan’s scores and stuff like that, I learned a lot. Space is very important.

Yes. If you look at a score and everybody’s playing all the time, you have trouble. But I know in the past I’ve had instances where I look at a score I’ve written and, especially if it’s for a large group, and, “Gee I haven’t written anything for the bassoon in 20 measures, I’d better give him something to do.” And that is not really the way to think I guess.

No. Not at all. You have to think in colors and combinations. You know with the jazz big band you think you’d run out of colors but you don’t. You can always find new combinations. You could never use up all the devices.

It’s interesting you say that because I listened to one of your charts last night of your own band, and I jotted the name down and now I can’t find it, but it was like a swing chart and you had one trumpet player playing the melody with the sax section. And it was such a great effect. It was not totally obvious but it changed the sound of the melody. That was really cool.

Yeah I stole that from Thad Jones. Yeah Thad would always couple the flugelhorn with the lead alto and/or if the lead melody line in the saxes is a soprano sax, which is a very weak instrument, then he would couple the flugelhorn with the soprano in the melody and © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

it worked very well. Bill Stapleton, with Woody Herman’s band, he did that, he stole that from Thad too. We all stole from each other. But it’s interesting that if you couple things correctly, and it was a compliment you just paid me, that you can’t tell what it is, you just hear — it’s in there. You know.
Yeah. It’s a unique sound for that time. You must have transitioned, well I should say and ask, do you now use software, Finale or Sibelius or whatever?

Yeah I use Finale only because I can extract the parts. I hate copying parts. I can write faster with a score pad and pencil. I think Gordon Goodwin can as well and Mark Taylor as well. But after you’ve got the sketch done, for me now once I’ve got it in my head I just put it down in the computer and then you can extract the parts. Because that’s the hardest part is writing out the parts.
That’s for sure. But can you tell if using Finale has changed the way you write?

No it hasn’t. As a matter of fact when I was teaching, I just retired a few years ago, I would make it a point to all my students that you cannot use the playback of Finale or Sibelius or any of those. Do not listen to the playback. If you listen to a playback make everything piano. Because you’re going to get fooled because the instrument has no overtones. I’ve put in, just as an example for the kids, I’ve put in Thad Jones’s “Quietitude” I put that in Finale, I put in Gil Evans’s “My Ship,” I put that in Finale. And I’ve got the best sound libraries you can buy. All right? And I play it back to the kids. It sounds like crap. You wouldn’t dare write that, because that doesn’t sound right. And they hear the sounds, “Oh that’s not right” so they take it away. They’re afraid to put the sharp nine and the natural nine together, you know, in a dominant seven chord because the machine doesn’t like it you know. It sounds awful. So they won’t take a chance. And that’s the one thing I really pounded into their heads that you cannot do that. And no it doesn’t affect me but it might affect younger writers today. They might, you know, take the easy way out because the machine tells them that, or the sounds.
Plus the opportunities to sit in a big band and absorb all that information over the years is not there like it was unless you’re in an educational school —

Yep that’s right. I really bemoan the fact that there aren’t any bands for these kids to go out and get real training. I mean there’s nothing like being in a band, whether it be a small band or a big band, but big band, learning how to play in a section, how to balance, you know, how to listen. It’s really important.
As time goes by and terrific arrangers come and go, does it become harder to create something new?
